newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Brazil bidding is telecommunications "Olympics".
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Brazil bidding is telecommunications "Olympics".

text.p: A contest is under way for what the telecommunications business is calling "The Cellular Olympics". The prize -- concessions to provide cellular phone systems to Brazil's potentially vast market.
More than a dozen consortiums, among them U.S. firms BellSouth Corp and AT&T Corp, will put in bids at an auction of cellular "Band-B" concessions in Brasilia on April 7.
Down the road are even more lucrative wire line and long-distance concessions in what analysts say is one of the hottest sectors of President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's privatisation plans.

"The Brazilian telecommunications market is second in the world only to China in excitement," said William Beavington, analyst for Latin American telecommunications at Paribas Capital Markets in New York.

Brazil has a population of about 160 million but only about nine lines per 100 people, according to Latin Trade magazine. Rio de Janeiro and Sao Paulo reportedly have waiting lists for cell phones topping 1.5 million people.

The system, built up by Brazil's military rulers in the 1970s but allowed to fall into decline, is badly in need of money and modernisation. The going rate on the black market for a line is between $2,500 and $4,000, analysts say.
Roberto Peon, president of BellSouth's operations for Latin America, said bidding on April 7 would be very heavy.
Brazil's Communications Ministry, in its bid invitation, listed 10 concessions, two of which will be announced first.
Operators must prove they are capable of serving 1.8 million customers in each of the largest two concessions. How many terminals they eventually provide depends on them.
"Some people are calling it the Olympics of cellular phones," Peon told Reuters.
COMPETITION FOR POTENTIALLY HUGE MARKET
Among BellSouth's competition are consortiums involving AT&T, Airtouch, GTE and Millicom of the United States, Stet of Italy and Hutchison of Hong Kong. Foreign investors require local partners.
"There are very few of the big ones who are not mounting strong bids. We've been pursuing it for eight years. We've hung in there. It's a very big market for us," said Atlanta-based Peon.
Other interested parties were more reticent. "It's a very delicate moment. The joint venture doesn't want to say anything about the bidding because it could be misleading," said an AT&T spokeswoman.
The auction of the cellular concessions is a crucial precursor to future auctions of wire lines, Beavington said.
"A success in cellular auctions will be seen as a chance of success in winning wire line contracts," he said.
Evidence of the intense interest is the so-called "pop price" -- a fee companies must pay the government for the concessions, based on the population who live in them.
For Sao Paulo, the "jewel in the crown", it could go as high as $50 per head of population, Beavington said. That is almost double the highest "pop price" in the United States.
"This is an untapped market. The potential is huge," said Zain Manekia of analysts S.G. Warburg.
PRIVATISATION HAS COMPLEX LEGAL BACKGROUND
But the privatisation also involves a series of complex and still uncompleted legal workings against the backdrop of an economy which at times bobs up and down like a samba line.
"There are very little guidelines about what is happening and so many rumours," Manekia said.

Communications minister Sergio Motta said recently the national telecommunications monopoly Telebras would be divided into four units. The largest of the 27 state subsidiaries, Sao Paulo operator Telesp, would be sold off by year's end.

Constitutional changes allowing privatisation have had to be introduced and new telecommunications laws reducing the government's role to purely regulation are still before congress. The exact future role of Telbras is unclear.
Some key regulations need to be sorted out, Beavington said. One important point is what the inter-connection charges for piggy-backing calls are likely to be.
Unions and some left-wing groups also oppose the privatisation and have started legal challeges.

Manekia also said it was important that the government ensured that bids, both now and in the future, were handled in such a way to avoid choice areas such as Sao Paulo or Rio being snapped up while less attractive areas were ignored.
For the cellular concessions, the government appeared to be offering one prime area coupled with a "not-so-good area", a policy he said was wise.
BellSouth's Peon praised the government for the way it was handling the privatisation.
"The evolution has taken about two years, changing the constitution, coming up with new regulations," he said. "I'm convinced they are going to do it as fast as they can."
But he said Brazil's tax sytem was still a problem. Duty and VAT rates are very high.
"It is decreasing but that is a very important factor. The price of phones has to be reasonable."
Inflation was also a concern but the economy was not as volatile as before and Brazil's integration into trade blocs was a good sign, he said.

Beavington said although the economy was not entirely stable in the short term "that doesn't really matter because in the long term the market is so attractive people are prepared to put up with red tape and uncertainty."
